basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Sensitive topic (student mental health / suicide prevention): informative, supportive framing used throughout; the mortality statistic is stated once, respectfully, without graphic detail, and every slide from Part 3 onward points toward concrete help; the talk closes on the 1925 hotline number and an encouraging, agency-focused message. Facts and sources: 23.1% of university students showed depressive-emotion tendencies in a 2024 survey (June-Oct 2024, n=3,264) by the Counseling Psychologists Association, R.O.C. (中華民國諮商心理師公會全國聯合會); academic pressure and financial difficulty were the top-cited stress sources, future-planning pressure ranked highest across all year levels, third-year students reported the highest overall stress (Heho健康 2024 coverage; epochtimes.com 2024-12-22 report of the same survey). One university (National Chung Cheng University) staff-reported rise from ~6% to ~8-9% with clear depressive symptoms over a decade, used as one illustrative, attributed data point, not a national figure (ccu.edu.tw news page). MOHW mortality data: self-harm is the #2 leading cause of death among Taiwanese aged 15-24 (~25%), and the #1 cause of death for young women in that age band (~34.4%), as reported via the same ccu.edu.tw article citing MOHW statistics -- stated once, respectfully, no method/graphic detail. Student Guidance Law (學生輔導法) revised to move the required university student-to-professional-counselor ratio from 1:1200 to 1:900; MOE began adjusting subsidy budgets from Jan 2024; ~216 additional counseling positions estimated needed nationwide (udn.com 2024 and 2025 coverage). Retention problem: campus counselor positions often pay only ~NT$44,000/month on one-year contracts, making them hard to fill even when funded (twreporter.org, "大專心理師耗竭前的SOS"). Access gap: ~78.5% of students who might benefit do not use their campus counseling center, citing lack of time, distance, and privacy concerns (Heho健康, "大學生心理諮商需求高"). Psychological leave (心理假) exists at many Taiwanese universities but only ~7.5% of students have ever used it (epochtimes.com 2024 report, and ccu.edu.tw). 1925 hotline (依舊愛我): MOHW-run, free, 24/7, single number since Dec 2019 (previously 0800-788-995); documented call volume grew from 27,926 calls (2005) to 78,108 calls (2018, ~6,500/month), reaching ~8,000 calls/month by 2019 -- described in the script only as "has grown steadily for years," not with an unverified recent-year total (mohw.gov.tw hotline history pages). Stigma/help-seeking context: a national adolescent survey (兒福聯盟) found ~39% of youth who struggle emotionally tell no one, correlated with perceived stigma -- used as general context for why stigma, not only access, is part of the problem (udn.com 2024 coverage of 兒福聯盟 survey). No specific 2023-2025 hotline call total was found and confirmed, so none is stated as a precise figure. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: Take a moment and look around this room. Statistically, about one in four students here is carrying more stress than they let on. Researchers have actually measured this, not guessed at it.
slides.2: SDG 3 establishes the global objective of good health and well-being, and it covers the mind as much as the body. Taiwan has taken that seriously in law. This talk asks whether practice matches the promise.
slides.3: University life can look effortless from the outside, full of classes, clubs and friends. Underneath that surface, though, many students are quietly carrying a heavy weight. This talk is about what that weight actually looks like.
slides.4: A 2024 survey of university students found that 23.1 percent showed signs of depression. That share, researchers noted, has been climbing for roughly a decade. School stress and money worries topped the list of causes.
slides.5: Ask students where the pressure comes from, and two answers stand out: schoolwork and money. Third-year students report the biggest load of all, right before they have to plan their entire future.
slides.6: One statistic is uncomfortable to hear, but silence would make the situation worse. Among those between 15 and 24, deaths linked to self-harm now rank as the second leading cause. That is why this talk exists.
slides.7: The law has finally caught up here. Universities must now provide one professional counselor for every 900 students, down from 1,200. That change alone should mean real, trained help for students like you.
slides.8: One number is worth memorising: 1925. It connects you to a free, 24-hour hotline that has quietly grown busier every year since it launched. Someone is always there on the other end, ready to listen.
slides.9: Psychological leave now exists on paper at many schools. It gives a struggling student the choice to step back, without any stigma. Whether students actually use it is another question, one the next few slides explore.
slides.10: On paper, fixing the ratio looks easy: simply hire more staff. Turning that into reality costs considerable money, though, and schools without enough budget will struggle to keep the new positions filled.
slides.11: Nobody stuck in a crisis should have to wait for a scheduled appointment slot. Evening hours, an online chat line or a quiet drop-in space would all lower that wait. Easier access can genuinely save lives.
slides.12: Rather than waiting for a crisis, universities can build prevention into normal classes. Teaching students to notice warning signs in themselves and their friends could spare someone real pain later.
slides.13: If these new positions stay unfilled, the improved ratio would exist only on paper. It would not yet exist in the room. Low pay on a one-year contract is usually why counselors are hard to keep.
slides.14: More counselors alone will not solve this problem completely. A large share of students who could genuinely benefit stay away, even when help is there. Time, distance and privacy worries all get in the way.
slides.15: Very few students take the psychological leave on the books. Roughly 7.5 percent actually do, according to one count. Having a right on paper is not the same as feeling free enough to use it.
slides.16: Two separate gaps sit side by side here. One is about capacity, enough trained staff, and the other is about comfort, feeling safe enough to ask. Fixing only one genuinely leaves the other wide open.
slides.17: Take stock of the complete picture for a moment. Taiwan can now point to a stronger law, a working hotline and genuine leave policies. Yet staffing gaps and quiet stigma keep pulling that progress backward.
slides.18: Nobody is asking you to fix the entire system by tomorrow. Simply noticing that a friend seems different and asking how they are doing counts as something real. A sincere question can matter a great deal.
slides.19: Warning signs are often genuinely subtle: less sleep, less energy, gradually drifting away from friends. Knowing them matters, but so does knowing the number to call afterward, 1925. Saying it out loud could genuinely help.
slides.20: Reaching out for help is not weakness. It is strength, and it takes genuine courage to admit that you are struggling. Help exists right now, completely free, and one number connects you to it: 1925.
